text.content:
Phase 4 is the long climax of the surface investigation — the end of Act I, not the end of the module. The party arrives in Rel Astra carrying everything Phase 3 produced and walks into the city the conspiracy actually operates from. Their job in this phase is to identify the three commissioner candidates the conspiracy intends to seat on Rel Astra's harbor commission, and to either stop the seating, indict Tarlith Vhal Sereth in Aerdi court, or remove him from play.

When this is — and how long is left

Phase 4 opens in spring 585 CY. The party rode out of Loftwick in autumn 584, spent the winter working Hardby, and crossed to Rel Astra in late winter. A fast table (relay to Hardby, packet east) can arrive as early as late winter 585; a delegation behind the councilman's carriage will not land before early summer. Nothing in the phase breaks either way, but every vacancy duration and every "years ago" on these pages is written for spring 585 — adjust once, at the top, if your table's itinerary ran long.

The conspiracy's outside date is autumn 586. It is written on the Third Seat's succession-deferral in the annotator's own hand — "Hold open until the second autumn after the next" — and from where the party is standing it is about eighteen months away. That is the wall behind the whole rest of the campaign, and Phase 4 is where the party first reads it without knowing what they are reading. Do not say "586" at the table. Let them do the arithmetic themselves, or not.

What this phase delivers

  • The shape of the conspiracy in operation. Phase 3 named the firm. Phase 4 names the three seats and the candidates intended for them. The party will be able to draw a clean diagram by the end, and will know which candidate is the weak link.
  • A confrontation with Tarlith Vhal Sereth. Three viable resolutions: legal indictment in Aerdi commercial court (slow, public, certain if the deposition holds); private removal (the party can leverage what they know to force his exit and a sealed succession at the firm); or kinetic removal (this is Rel Astra and Sereth has bodyguards, but it's not impossible — the cost is that the conspiracy buries the documentary trail and the party gains a reputation they will not lose).
  • The Aerdy claimant. The conspiracy is positioning the harbor revenue for one specific Naelax claimant to inherit at the next succession. Phase 4 names him. (Default: Lord Galenix Naelax, a cousin of the current Overking, currently in Rel Astra under a politely restrictive house-arrest by his political opponents.)
  • The first whisper of "E." Veska's three observations about how the letter was formed will, in Rel Astra, find a second instance — a registry document whose annotation is in the same hand. Phase 4 does not name Eclavdra. Phase 4 does not even confirm the writer is non-human. It only lets the party assemble a fourth and fifth observation, and notice that the writer is not, by any conventional reading, an Aerdy hand.

What this phase does NOT deliver

  • The Drow city is not named. The Vault is not visited.
  • The reason behind the operation — why the eastern harbor revenue matters to the writer of the marginalia — is not stated. The party may infer.
  • The succession itself does not occur in this campaign. The Wars do not begin in this campaign. The conspiracy is positioned for an event that has not yet happened.

Tier and DC assumptions

Tier 2–3 (levels 7–11). Investigation DCs cap at 18, social DCs at 17. The big combat encounter (the Sereth confrontation, kinetic version) is calibrated for a five-PC level-9 party with appropriate gear — the table this campaign is actually written for. Scaling for four or six is in The Sereth Confrontation > Path 3 — Kinetic Removal; a party of four will struggle and should expect a PC down.

Pacing — two tempos

Phase 4 runs on two clocks, and confusing them is the easiest way to break this phase. The first is the city: ten to twelve days of active play, the same on every path. The second is the court: a procedural tail that exists only on Path 1, runs another two months, and is played almost entirely in summary and correspondence. Do not number them as one continuous count.

Tempo one — the city (active play, about twelve days)

  1. Day 1–2: Arrival, settling into Rel Astra, first contact with Caelith's Rel Astra correspondent (see NPCs).
  2. Day 3–6: Investigation of the three commissioner candidates; identify the weak link. The registry visit and the fourth "E." observation land in this window.
  3. Day 5–8: Approach to Sereth (one of three paths). On Path 1 this is where Halask accepts the brief — and that day, not arrival day, is Path 1's Day 1.
  4. Day 7–10: The confrontation. Resolution.
  5. Day 9–12: Departure / aftermath on Paths 2 and 3. Caelith's final letter. The "E." thread is closed for this campaign and opened for the next.

Tempo two — the court (Path 1 only, summary play)

Path 1's timeline in The Sereth Confrontation is counted from the day Halask accepts the brief, normally city-day 5 to 8. From there: four days of preparation, the filing on its Day 5, a week of motions, eighteen days of depositions, and the preliminary hearing on its Day 29 — at which the harbor commission suspends candidate selection and the party is free to leave. The trial follows sixty days after that and reaches them by post.

Play the deposition window at whatever grain the table wants; it is where the Pressure Clock does its worst work, and it is the only stretch of Phase 4 that rewards a party for staying put. If the Hardby branch material was never secured in Phase 3, add ten days at the front for the Solen Mereth subpoena.

In short: a Path 2 or Path 3 table finishes Phase 4 in about twelve days of game time. A Path 1 table finishes active play in about the same, then spends five to six more weeks in the city on procedure before riding west. Both are correct. Phase 5 opens whenever they get home, and the road home is long enough that the difference washes out.

The Pressure Clock for Phase 4 is shorter (four segments) but the segments hit harder; see Phase 4 Pressure Clock. Note that its per-day trigger stops running once the indictment is filed — Path 1 is not built to burn down its own clock.

Tactical Map

Rel Astra — city map. Old Harbor Ward south of the harbor; Customs Quay north; Naelax embassy on the western edge of the Old City.

The Brass Sextant. Caelith's letter is the door.

Read aloud as the party reaches Rel Astra. Use this version only if they took the Lacquer Wave from Hardby — Phase 3's Route 2, the merchantman: seven weeks, forty-eight days, Old Harbor.

On the morning of the forty-eighth day out of Hardby, the Lacquer Wave makes her turn into the Old Harbor with the wind on her port quarter and the Aerdi sun already high enough to burn the haze off the water. Seven weeks. Half a dozen small ports you could not name if asked, and one long stretch of open water with nothing to do but read what you took out of the branch. You see Rel Astra a long while before you reach her — the city climbs the rise above the harbor in tiers of pale stone and warm tile, the four-story counting houses of the Goldsmiths' Quarter prominent on the eastern slope, the older quarter to the west crowded with red-roofed warrens, and the imperial walls of the Old Harbor Ward grey-faced and long.

The harbor itself is a working port. Three Aerdi galleys lie at the imperial moorings to the east; a half-dozen smaller hulls are berthed along the merchant quays; a single Yeomanry-flagged coaster (you do not know her) is moored on the far side of the basin. The lighthouse at the harbor's mouth — a square stone tower three stories tall, weathered by four centuries of salt — flies the current Aerdi imperial standard and beneath it, smaller, the white-and-blue swallow-tail of the Old Harbor Ward.

Captain Yorra Mel does not bring the Lacquer Wave to the imperial mooring. She slides her into a working berth on the merchant quay, hands you your half-fares back, says "Good business, then," and turns to her own paperwork without watching you go. She has done this for you before; she will do it again.

The harbor clerk who comes down the quay to check passengers takes your false names (or your real ones, depending on what you wrote on the manifest), copies them carefully into a bound register, hands you back the small silver tag you'll need for your return passage, and waves you up the quay toward the city. The whole transaction takes less than three minutes. Rel Astra, this morning, has not been told to look for you.

It is the eleventh hour. The Goldsmiths' Quarter clock — the city's master clock, set in the tower above the merchants' guild hall — is just chiming the hour. The harbor's clock and the imperial clock and the merchants' clock all chime together. They keep the same time. Rel Astra is older than that and has had time to fix what Hardby never bothered to fix.

What's true on this approach

  • The firm has been expecting them for two and a half weeks, and does not know they have landed. Hardby's dispatch about what the party did to the branch went out on a faster hull and reached Rel Astra roughly eighteen days ahead of them; Cindren & Vhal have had that long to prepare and are ready. What the party still holds is the moment of arrival: a trader files a cargo manifest, not a passenger list, so nobody at the quay writes down who came ashore. The firm knows they are coming. It does not know they are here, or on which hull, and it will be a day or two before a paid ear in the Old Harbor Ward supplies the answer.
  • Their evidence package is intact and concealed in the Lacquer Wave's cargo manifest as wool. They can collect it from Yorra at any time in the next three days; she will hold it without asking why.
  • They arrive in the Old Harbor Ward — Rel Astra's harbor district, its commercial heart, and the district where Cindren & Vhal Rel Astra has its main counting house. They are inside the conspiracy's home district from the moment they step off the gangway.
  • Caelith's Rel Astra correspondent — a retired Aerdi advocate named Therion Halask, see NPCs — keeps morning hours at the Brass Sextant coffee-house on the third quay. The party may approach him today.

District Map

Old Harbor Ward. The party's arrival point by sea (Lacquer Wave to merchant quays); also the home of Belven Astor's chandlery on Wave-and-Anchor Square.

The Brass Sextant. Caelith's letter is the door — and on this route the party gets there first.

Read aloud as the party reaches Rel Astra. Use this version only if they bought berths on the mail packet out of Hardby — Phase 3's Route 1: four and a half weeks, thirty days, Customs Quay. This is the only arrival that beats the news.

Thirty days, and the packet has not stopped for anything that was not the mails. Fresh crew at Saltmarsh, a night watch that sailed straight through weather the Lacquer Wave would have anchored out, and bunks that have taught each of you something about your own spine. On the morning of the thirtieth day the mail packet comes up on Rel Astra from the south-east with her signal flags already flying, and does not slow for the harbor.

The city climbs the rise above the water in tiers of pale stone and warm tile — the four-story counting houses of the Goldsmiths' Quarter prominent on the eastern slope, the older quarter west of them crowded with red-roofed warrens, the grey imperial walls of the Old Harbor Ward long and low along the shore. You have been looking at it, on and off, for the better part of an hour. It does not look like a city that has been waiting for you.

It has not been. That is the whole point of the fare you paid.

The packet berths at the Customs Quay, north side, at the imperial mail stage, and the mail goes off her before the passengers do — two sealed pouches carried at a jog by a customs runner who does not look at any of you. Somewhere in one of those pouches is Hardby's dispatch about what you did to the branch. It will be on a desk in the Goldsmiths' Quarter by this afternoon, or tomorrow morning at the latest, and there is nothing to be done about that except to have arrived on the same hull.

The customs clerk who takes your names does it properly: a bound register, a careful hand, the travelling names you gave in Hardby copied out in full, a silver return-passage tag pressed into each palm. It takes a quarter of an hour. It is a document of record, and it is read at both ends.

The Aerdi sun is high. The city smells of lemon and dust and clean salt. Below the Customs House the harbor's clock chimes the eleventh hour, and every other clock in Rel Astra chimes with it — the imperial, the merchants', the ward's, all together, all correct. Rel Astra is older than Hardby and has had the time to fix what Hardby never bothered to fix.

What's true on this approach

  • The party arrives with the news, not behind it. Hardby's dispatch about the branch is in the mail pouches that came off the same hull. Cindren & Vhal Rel Astra will read it today or tomorrow, not eighteen days ago. Everything the firm does in Phase 4, it does from a standing start. This is the single largest tactical advantage available in the phase, and it lasts about a day and a half.
  • And the firm has their names before they have breakfast. The packet carries the mails, so the passenger list is a document of record read by the harbour authority at both ends; the party is written down. They have bought surprise about Hardby at the cost of any anonymity about themselves. A party that assumed a fast ship meant a quiet one should learn otherwise from a polite note delivered to their lodgings on the second day.
  • A PC who thinks to ask what else is in the mail bag is asking a very good question. Halask can, with two days and a favour, learn what came east on that packet besides them. The answer is: Hardby's dispatch, the harbor commission's routine correspondence, and one sealed cover for Sereth's office that nobody will let them look at.
  • Their evidence package travelled in their own baggage under their own eyes — there was no hold to hide it in and no wool bale to fold it into. It has been searched once, at Saltmarsh, by a bored imperial customs officer who found nothing because there was nothing on that day's list to look for. It is intact. It has also been handled.
  • They arrive at the Customs Quay, on the wrong side of the city — correct, documented, and a long walk from the Old Harbor Ward and the conspiracy's front door. Budget the first afternoon for crossing Rel Astra on foot with everything they own.
  • Caelith's Rel Astra correspondent — a retired Aerdi advocate named Therion Halask, see NPCs — keeps morning hours at the Brass Sextant coffee-house on the third quay. He is not expecting them this early. The party has outrun Caelith's own correspondence — the letter telling Halask they were coming is still at sea behind them. Halask will be visibly recalculating for the first ten minutes of the conversation, and will say so, because he is that kind of man. See Caelith's Continuing Letters: on this route, Letter 4 has not landed yet.

District Map

Customs Quay district. The packet berths at the imperial mail stage on the north side; the Old Harbor Ward is a long walk south.

By morning of the second day, the party is expected at the Brass Sextant.

Read aloud as the party reaches Rel Astra. Use this version only if they rode the old coastal road from Hardby — Phase 3's Route 3 on horseback: eight and a half weeks, sixty days, West Gate.

You crest the last low ridge sixty days out of Hardby and Rel Astra opens below you in the late-afternoon light: a long arc of pale stone curving inland from the bay, the four-story counting houses on the eastern slope catching the sun, the imperial walls of the Old Harbor Ward grey and shadowed at this hour, and beyond the city the open Aerdi sea, blue going to copper at the horizon.

The road from the west drops down into a switchback through olive groves and scrub, and joins the West Gate caravan road two miles out. By the time you reach the gate, you are riding in a thin afternoon traffic of cart-drovers, returning fishermen with empty creels, and a single Aerdi imperial courier on a fresh horse who passes you without looking back.

The West Gate is the imperial gate of Rel Astra — older than the city's commercial walls, set in a deep barbican, manned by Aerdi imperial guards in the oxblood-and-gold of the current Overking's household. The corporal who reviews your papers (your false-name papers, or whatever you carry) glances at them, glances at the party, asks one perfunctory question about your business, and waves you through. The Aerdi imperial gate-watch is, famously, very fast and very disinterested. Whoever it is the conspiracy has paid in this city, it is not the imperial gate-watch.

Inside the West Gate, you are immediately in the Old City — a tangle of stepped streets, herb-vendors, basket-makers, three temples of three separate Aerdi deities each ringing a different evening bell. You can see the rise of the Goldsmiths' Quarter to the east, four-story counting houses cresting the next slope. The Old Harbor Ward is below them, and the harbor below that.

You have arrived on the evening of the sixtieth day. Fourteen hundred and fifty miles of road are behind you and none of it is in your legs any more; it is somewhere further in than that. It is not yet dark. The clocks of Rel Astra all begin to chime the seventh hour, together, the way the clocks of Hardby never quite managed.

What's true on this approach

  • The party arrived overland and the West Gate has not particularly noticed them. The imperial gate-roster will note their entry only by paper, not by name, and the conspiracy's network does not extend to it. They have a clean entry and are not yet observed.
  • The firm has had a month's warning and does not know they have landed. Hardby's dispatch went east by sea and beat them here by roughly thirty days; Cindren & Vhal are prepared and waiting. What the road bought is the arrival itself: no quay, no harbour authority, no passenger list, no document anywhere. The party is the only one of the four routes that enters Rel Astra without generating a piece of paper. If they took the road under Commercial Cover and survived the day-three blade attempt, the conspiracy in Hardby knows they tried and does not know they made it; Cindren-aligned ears in Rel Astra will not hear of them for a day and a half.
  • If they travelled under Official Delegation they were not on horseback at all — they were behind the councilman's carriage, which is another twenty days and its own read-aloud (Arrival — Customs Quay). Do not run both. A delegation does not overtake its own carriage.
  • Their evidence package is in their saddlebags and is the most exposed it has been since Hardby; recommend they offload to Therion Halask (see NPCs) within their first forty-eight hours.

The full party at the Customs Quay. The Aerdi delegation waits formally; the Hall of the Compass and the harbor are visible behind.

Even under diplomatic seal, the morning visit to the Brass Sextant happens.

Read aloud as the party reaches Rel Astra. Use this version only if they travelled behind the councilman's carriage — Phase 3's Route 3 under Official Delegation: eleven and a half weeks, eighty days, Customs Quay.

The diplomatic carriage rolls through Rel Astra's Customs Quay gate on the morning of the eightieth day out of Hardby. Eighty days at the pace of a man who will not be hurried and cannot be touched, through every provincial courtesy the Aerdi southern road can produce. There has been a small Aerdi delegation waiting at the quay since dawn — three minor functionaries from the Old Harbor Ward Council, two clerks from the harbor commission, a single liveried herald in oxblood and gold who delivers the bows of formal welcome.

The councilman steps down from the lead carriage. The bows are exchanged. The clerks hand him a folded card listing the audiences arranged for the next nine days: an audience with the Old Harbor Ward Council on the third day; a courtesy reception at the harbor commission on the fifth; an opportunity to present credentials at the Goldsmiths' Hall on the seventh; and on the morning of the ninth day, a private interview with the senior partner of Cindren & Vhal Rel Astra — Tarlith Vhal Sereth — at his offices.

You are then escorted, in the same procession, through the imperial-style streets of the Old Harbor Ward to the formal lodgings prepared for the delegation: the Hall of the Compass, a three-story Aerdi guest residence on the Customs Quay, two streets from the harbor commission's hall and three streets from Sereth's office. The hall is staffed by Aerdi imperial servants and is, you understand without anyone needing to say so, comprehensively under observation by every faction in the city that has an interest in why a Yeomanry delegation has come to Rel Astra at this season.

The Aerdi sun is high. The city smells of lemon, dust, and clean salt water. Below the windows of the Hall of the Compass, the harbor's clock chimes ten, and every other clock in Rel Astra chimes with it.

What's true on this approach

  • The party has full diplomatic standing. They cannot be detained, they cannot be harassed, they cannot be physically attacked without an act-of-war level incident. This protection is the entire reason this approach was worth the speed cost.
  • The party has a scheduled private interview with Tarlith Vhal Sereth on the ninth day. This audience does not happen on any other approach. The price they paid for the audience is eleven and a half weeks. The delegation was announced to every Aerdi authority east of Hardby before it left, and the conspiracy has had the entire crossing to prepare — and used it. This is why the Pressure Clock opens at two segments on this approach.
  • The court-issued warrant from Hardby (if they obtained one in Phase 3 Path 3) can be presented to the harbor commission and executed at C&V Rel Astra by Aerdi watch on the seventh day. The harbor commission will slow-walk the procedure as much as it can; the warrant will execute, but every locked drawer will have been emptied.
  • The councilman is, as ever, polite, formal, slow, and reporting back to his own faction by every dispatch. The party should plan to operate around him, not through him.
  • Their evidence package is in formal diplomatic dispatch cases under imperial seal. It is also being read by every Aerdi imperial intelligence officer in the city. Recommend they brief Therion Halask the morning after arrival.

District Map

Customs Quay district. The party's arrival point under formal accreditation; the Hall of the Compass is the diplomatic guesthouse.

Three more letters from Caelith reach the party in Rel Astra. None of them is a reply to anything the party does there, and none of them can be.

Caelith writes to Therion Halask every two weeks and has done since before the party left Loftwick; Halask keeps the stack in a drawer under his table at the Brass Sextant. Loftwick to Rel Astra is the relay to Hardby and then a hull east — seven or eight weeks one way, the better part of five months for a round trip — so every letter the party reads in this city was written about two months ago, by a man who did not yet know whether they had left Hardby alive. He knows the arithmetic. He writes anyway, and the letters show it.

Hand them over on pacing, not on a courier's arithmetic. Letter 4 at the first quiet moment after the party has met Halask; Letter 5 around the middle of the phase; Letter 6 at departure — or, if the phase ran short, let it catch them on the road west and read it aloud there. If a player asks whether Caelith knows what they have done in Rel Astra: no. He will not know for two months. That is the shape of Phase 4, and it is why Halask matters so much.

[If the party took the fast packet:] They outran their own mail. Letter 4 has not arrived when they land, and Halask says so, apologetically, with the drawer open to prove it. Hold Letter 4 until the phase's second week; it comes in on the next packet, addressed in a hand they know, having been written before any of this started.

Letter 4 — within three days of arrival

Yours from Hardby's last post-house reached me in the third week after you sailed (or rode, or were carried in the councilman's carriage; you had not told me which, and I refrained from reading the harbor news for the pleasure of being told by you). By the time you read this I expect the pleasure has gone stale. Write anyway.

Two things you should know.

First — the original of Veska's notarial opinion is in Trina's strongroom. Trina has read it. She has decided, on her own initiative and without consulting me, to send a sealed copy by separate courier to a person she names only as "my old correspondent in the wood." I do not know who this is. I have not asked. Trina trusts what Trina trusts. The opinion will, by some path, find at least one set of eyes that no Aerdi or Yeomanry court will ever recognize as having read it. Whether this matters to you, on the ground in Rel Astra, depends on what you do next.

Second — Brane's Civic Reconciliation Closure motion passed in the Council on the seventh day after you sailed. The matter of Haskur Vandrell is, in Loftwick civic record, declared resolved. The Audit Hall has formally withdrawn clerical support from any further inquiry into the Vandrell matter. This means I am writing to you privately and on my own paper. I am still in the post. I no longer have any standing in it. I cannot direct an inquiry; I can only correspond with people who are conducting one. Anything you accomplish in Rel Astra, you accomplish on the strength of what you can prove in Aerdi court, not on the strength of any letter I can write you.

Halask is the man you want. He will not be the man you expect.

— C.

Letter 5 — about a week into Phase 4

The clerk in my office is named Ostren Pell. I have known this for nineteen days. I have done nothing about it. He continues to come to work. He continues to forward my correspondence wherever he forwards it. I am keeping him in place because his removal would tell whoever pays him that I know, and I would prefer they continue to believe that I do not.

This is not a position I am proud of. I tell you because, in Rel Astra, you may be tempted to reason from the corruption you can see to the corruption you cannot. Sometimes the people who know are the ones who appear to be doing nothing. Treat Halask under this rule. Treat the Old Harbor Ward Council members under this rule. Treat anyone in the harbor commission who has done you a small public courtesy under this rule.

I have one piece of news from outside Loftwick. The Yeomanry's quiet contact in the Domain of Greyhawk — not someone I know personally, but someone whose name comes up in correspondence I am not supposed to read — has sent word that a man fitting Haskur Vandrell's description was seen, briefly, in Greyhawk City three weeks ago, in the company of a younger man the contact did not recognize. The younger man wore no rings and no insignia. The contact, who has good eyes for these things, says the younger man's gait was not Aerdi and not Yeomanry. I tell you this for what it is worth, which may be very little. If Vandrell is alive and on the move with a successor in tow, that may shape what you do with Sereth.

Trina sends her regards, and asked me twice to be sure I had written them down.

— C.

Letter 6 — toward the end of Phase 4

If you have read this and not yet written me back, then I assume Sereth is either indicted, removed, or dead, and the matter of the three commissioners is settled one way or another.

I will not ask which.

I will only say this. The conspiracy you have named is not the conspiracy. The conspiracy is positioned to take advantage of the next Aerdy succession, and the next Aerdy succession will happen, and the harbor commission will sit, and a name you have not yet heard will be the name that sits behind whichever Naelax cousin wins the iron crown. Three commissioners, three votes that move together first, and a great deal of patience. Whoever drew this plan drew it ten years ago.

The annotation Veska could not place. You will, in Rel Astra, find a second instance of it. Possibly a third. Notice the small details — the nib, the wax, the dates it chooses. Do not pursue the writer. The writer is not in Rel Astra, and you do not have a country to look in, let alone a name; a man who chases a hand across a map arrives everywhere late and learns nothing on the way. I do not know who the writer is. I know only what a hand looks like that has not spent its life under Aerdi or Yeomanry sun. I have seen one like it once, twenty years ago, on a document I was not meant to be holding, and I did not learn then whose it was either. Collect the observations. Do not spend the phase on them.

Come home alive. We will talk.

— C.
